title: Arpinum to the Rostra: the Voice of the Republic
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Arpinum and the Making of an Orator

stops.name: Arpinum, the villa on the Fibrenus
stops.campa: On the third of January, in the hill country of the Volsci, Marcus Tullius Cicero is born into an equestrian family at the villa where the cold Fibrenus forks around a wooded island before it joins the Liris below Arpinum. He will remember this ground all his life, the plane trees, the little island where he and his brother Quintus will one day walk debating law and the stars. Arpinum gave Rome the soldier Gaius Marius a generation before; it gives Rome now a second son, who will conquer not by the sword but by the tongue.
suggested_refs: The site of Cicero's family villa near Isola del Liri, at the confluence of the Fibrenus and the Liris, described by Cicero himself in De Legibus II
sources: The Princeton Encyclopedia of Classical Sites, s.v. Arpinum

stops.name: Rome, the Forum — the tirocinium under Scaevola
stops.campa: Cicero takes the toga of manhood and his father brings him to Rome and attaches him to Quintus Mucius Scaevola the augur, the most learned jurist of the age, that he may learn law by standing at his side. He never leaves the old man while he lives, and after his death he attaches himself in the same way to Scaevola the pontifex, his cousin. In the Forum he listens to the consultations of citizens, watches the give and take of the courts, and begins the long apprenticeship of the ear and the tongue that will make him Rome's first voice.
suggested_refs: The Roman Forum, where the two Scaevolae gave counsel and where Cicero began his tirocinium fori

stops.name: The Social War — the camp of Pompeius Strabo
stops.campa: Rome's Italian allies rise in revolt and Cicero, not yet twenty, serves his first campaign in the tent of the consul Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo before Asculum. It is a hard, close war fought against neighbors, and Cicero later says he learned there what war truly costs. In the same camp serves the consul's son, a young man of his own age named Gnaeus Pompeius, called in time Magnus, whose fortune will cross Cicero's own for the rest of both their lives, in the Forum, in the field, and at the last on opposite shores of a civil war.
suggested_refs: The siege lines before Asculum (modern Ascoli Piceno) in the Social War of 91-88 BC

stops.name: Rome — Philo of Larissa and the arrival of the Academy
stops.campa: Driven from Athens by Mithridates' war, Philo, the head of Plato's own Academy, comes to Rome and opens his lectures to the city. Cicero, seized as he says by an extraordinary zeal for philosophy, gives himself over entirely to him, drinking in the doctrine of the New Academy, that the wise man may argue either side of any question and hold no opinion as certain. It is a habit of mind he never loses: the same suspension of dogma that will let him defend, prosecute, and later meditate every school of Greek thought without ever quite belonging to one.
suggested_refs: Philo of Larissa's lectures in Rome, 88-87 BC, the seed of Cicero's lifelong Academic skepticism

segments.name: Pro Roscio and the Prudent Withdrawal

stops.name: Rome, the Forum — Pro Roscio Amerino
stops.campa: At twenty-six, in Sulla's Rome, Cicero rises to defend Sextus Roscius of Ameria against a charge of parricide brought by men close to the dictator's freedman Chrysogonus, who has already carved up the murdered father's estate among himself. It is a dangerous case and no other advocate will touch it. Cicero wins it, and in doing so quotes old Lucius Cassius, whom the people called the wisest and most honest of judges, who always asked of any crime a single question first.
stops.quote: Cui bono fuerit — to whose benefit was it?
suggested_refs: The text of Pro Roscio Amerino, Cicero's first great criminal defense, delivered in 80 BC

stops.name: Athens — the garden of the Academy
stops.campa: Cicero leaves Rome, giving out that he goes for his health, though friends know Sulla's enmity is not yet spent. He crosses to Athens and sits again under philosophers, this time Antiochus of Ascalon, who is turning the Academy back toward the certainties Philo had loosened. He walks the Academy's own garden, visits the tomb of Plato, and studies with his cousin Lucius and with Atticus, who has made his home in the city and will remain his dearest friend and correspondent for the rest of both their lives.
suggested_refs: Plato's Academy at Athens, where Cicero studied under Antiochus of Ascalon in 79 BC

stops.name: Rhodes — Apollonius Molon and the tears of the Greek master
stops.campa: From Asia, where he hears the rhetors of Adramyttium and Caria and Halicarnassus, Cicero comes at last to Rhodes to study under Apollonius Molon, the reigning master of declamation, and also attends the Stoic Posidonius. Not understanding Latin, Molon asks him to declaim in Greek, so that his faults may be corrected; when he finishes, every listener praises him but Molon sits silent and grave a long while, then speaks the words the school will repeat for centuries after, of admiration for the pupil and pity for the teacher's own exhausted country.
suggested_refs: The rhetorical school of Apollonius Molon at Rhodes, where Cicero and, a generation later, Julius Caesar both studied
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History XLVI.18 (on Molon's fame)

stops.name: Rome — return, marriage to Terentia, the quaestorship won
stops.campa: Two years abroad have changed his voice: the strained, overheated style of the Roscius case has been worked down by exercise and by Molon's discipline into something fuller in the chest and cooler in judgment. He returns to Rome thinner, his health mended, and resumes practice at the bar with a name already made. Terentia, of a well-off family, whom he married about the time he set out, brings a dowry and a will as forceful as his own. Standing for the quaestorship, the first rung of the senatorial ladder, he is elected by every century of the Roman people.
suggested_refs: Cicero's marriage to Terentia, contracted c. 80-77 BC, and his election to the quaestorship for 75 BC

stops.name: Lilybaeum, Sicily — quaestor
stops.campa: Cicero sails to western Sicily as quaestor under the propraetor Sextus Peducaeus, charged with the grain supply out of Lilybaeum in a year of scarcity. He governs so scrupulously, he says, that the Sicilians treat him ever after as their own advocate at Rome. Returning by way of Puteoli, he meets a Roman acquaintance who asks what news from Rome, assuming he means the capital, and is astonished to learn the young man has been abroad on the state's business at all. Cicero takes the lesson to heart: reputation must be renewed at Rome, or Rome forgets it.
suggested_refs: Lilybaeum (modern Marsala), Cicero's quaestorian province in western Sicily, 75 BC

stops.name: Syracuse — the forgotten tomb of Archimedes
stops.campa: As quaestor Cicero goes up to Syracuse and asks to see the tomb of Archimedes, dead a hundred and thirty-seven years. The Syracusans know nothing of it and deny any such thing exists. But Cicero remembers a few verses said to be carved there, describing a sphere and a cylinder set upon the stone, and he searches the ground by the Agrigentine Gate until, in a thicket of briars and thorn, he finds a small column rising just above the scrub, bearing the very figures. He orders the brush cut back and stands before the grave the city itself had let vanish.
stops.quote: I remembered certain verses inscribed, as I had heard, on his tomb, and these set forth that a sphere and a cylinder had been put on the top of the grave. So I looked all around, for there are a great quantity of tombs at the Agrigentine Gate, and finally I noted a small column standing out a little above the brambles, on which there was the figure of a sphere and a cylinder.
suggested_refs: The sphere-and-cylinder tomb marker of Archimedes, rediscovered by Cicero near Syracuse's Agrigentine Gate, 75 BC

stops.name: Rome, the Forum — the prosecution of Verres
stops.campa: The Sicilians, remembering their honest quaestor, ask Cicero to prosecute Gaius Verres, their late governor, for three years of extortion, theft of Greek statues and paintings, and the judicial murder of Roman citizens. Verres retains Hortensius, the greatest advocate then living, and counts on delay to run past a friendly jury pool. Cicero breaks the strategy by gathering the evidence himself in Sicily in fifty days and opening with a short, devastating actio prima; Verres does not wait for the second round of speeches but flees to Massilia before Cicero can deliver them, taking his stolen art with him into exile.
stops.quote: Facinus est vincire civem Romanum, scelus verberare, prope parricidium necare: quid dicam in crucem tollere? — It is a crime to bind a Roman citizen, a sin to scourge him, almost an act of parricide to kill him; what shall I say of crucifying him?
suggested_refs: The Verrine Orations, and the looted Sicilian art collection that made Verres notorious

stops.name: Tusculum — the villa purchased
stops.campa: With the fees and fame the Verres case brings him, Cicero buys a villa on the slope above the old Latin town of Tusculum, in the hills southeast of Rome, on ground once graced, tradition says, by Sulla himself. Modeled in part on the gymnasia of Athens, it becomes his true home, the place he returns to write, to grieve, and to think, more than any house in the capital. Here in the years ahead he will build his own Academy and Lyceum in miniature, walk the colonnades in argument with his friends, and compose the dialogues that carry Greek philosophy into Latin.
suggested_refs: The Tusculanum, Cicero's philosophical retreat near modern Frascati, purchased c. 68 BC
sources: D'Arms, Romans on the Bay of Naples (on villa culture)

stops.name: Rome — praetor, De Imperio Cn. Pompei
stops.campa: Elected praetor at the earliest legal age, Cicero delivers from the Rostra his first speech before the full assembly of the people, urging that command against Mithridates be given to Pompey with unprecedented, unlimited power. It is a calculated alliance: he attaches his rising name to the greatest soldier of the age, and the law passes overwhelmingly. He governs his court honestly through the year, and looks now, at forty, toward the consulship itself, the summit no man of his family, a mere knight of Arpinum with no consular ancestor, has ever before reached at Rome.
suggested_refs: The Rostra in the Roman Forum, where De Imperio Cn. Pompei was delivered, 66 BC

stops.name: Rome — elected consul, first of his family
stops.campa: Against nobles of ancient consular houses and against Catiline, a patrician of ruined fortune and worse repute, Cicero is returned consul for the coming year by every century of the centuriate assembly, a novus homo, the first new man to reach the consulship in thirty years and the first ever from Arpinum. It is the summit of the cursus honorum, and he takes it, he will say later, not for the ivory chair or the lictors' rods but so that he might one day be able to say he had saved the republic that raised him.
suggested_refs: The consular elections of 64 BC and Cicero's status as novus homo, the first of his family to reach the consulship

stops.name: Rome, the Temple of Jupiter Stator — the First Catilinarian
stops.campa: Warned of a plot to murder him and burn the city, Cicero convenes the Senate not in its house but in the well-guarded Temple of Jupiter Stator on the Palatine slope, and there, with Catiline himself seated among the senators who draw away from him on every side, delivers the first and most famous of his four Catilinarian orations. Rome has never heard anything like it: the conspirator denounced to his face, in his hearing, while the machinery of state closes around him. That night Catiline leaves the city for his army gathering in Etruria, and never returns to it alive.
stops.quote: Quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra? — How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?
suggested_refs: The Temple of Jupiter Stator on the Palatine, traditional site of the First Catilinarian Oration

stops.name: Rome, the Tullianum — the conspirators strangled
stops.campa: The Senate, moved by Cato's speech against Caesar's plea for mercy, votes death for the five conspirators taken in the city. Cicero himself, as consul, leads Lentulus by the hand down into the Tullianum, the old stone pit below the Capitol, where the public executioner is waiting; the others follow under praetorian guard. When it is done he turns to the crowd still massed in the Forum in the winter dark and pronounces, with the plain finality of a man announcing weather, the single word that will be quoted against him for the rest of his life.
stops.quote_source: Reported by Plutarch, Life of Cicero 22
suggested_refs: The Tullianum (Mamertine Prison) beneath the Capitoline, where the Catilinarian conspirators were executed

stops.name: Rome, the Rostra — the oath at the laying down of the consulship
stops.campa: On the last day of the year the consul climbs the Rostra to make the customary farewell address, and the tribune Metellus Nepos, with Bestia beside him and the praetor Caesar behind them both, forbids it: a man who has put citizens to death untried shall not be heard, only sworn out of office. Cicero raises his hand and swears instead an oath no consul has sworn before, that he and he alone has saved this city and kept the republic standing. The whole assembly, with one voice, swears the same oath back to him, and he goes home through a crowd carrying torches.
stops.quote: I swear in very truth that I have saved my country and maintained her supremacy.
stops.quote_source: Reported by Plutarch, Life of Cicero 23
suggested_refs: The Rostra in the Roman Forum, where Cicero swore his own oath in place of the customary farewell address, 29 December 63 BC

stops.name: Rome — the Bona Dea trial, the enemy made
stops.campa: Publius Clodius Pulcher, a patrician of Cicero's own generation, slips in women's dress into the December rites of the Good Goddess, celebrated in the house of Caesar the pontifex maximus, where no man may look. Brought to trial for sacrilege in May, he swears he was ninety miles from Rome that night at Interamna. Cicero, called as a witness, testifies that Clodius had come to his own door in the city that very morning, and the alibi collapses. A bribed jury acquits him all the same, thirty-one votes to twenty-five. For the price of a true word Cicero has made the enemy who will unmake him.
suggested_refs: The Bona Dea sacrilege of December 62 BC and Clodius's acquittal in May 61 BC, the origin of his enmity toward Cicero

stops.name: Rome — departure into exile
stops.campa: Five years after the executions, the tribune Publius Clodius Pulcher, an old enemy, carries a law outlawing anyone who has put a Roman citizen to death without trial, aimed squarely at Cicero and the men of the Tullianum. Rather than stand a trial he believes rigged against him, and against the pleading of many friends, Cicero puts on the mourning dress of the accused, is deserted by the consuls who owe him their careers, and slips out of Rome by night toward Brundisium and the sea, leaving Terentia, his children, and every honor he has won behind him.
suggested_refs: The Lex Clodia de capite civis Romani, March 58 BC, and Cicero's flight into exile

stops.name: Thessalonica — the exile
stops.campa: Cicero crosses to Dyrrachium and settles for the worst months of his life at Thessalonica on the Via Egnatia, sheltered by the quaestor Plancius, who he says treats him like a brother. He cannot eat, cannot sleep, writes letters to Atticus that break off mid-sentence in tears, and begs Terentia and Tullia to bear up under a ruin he blames wholly on his own misjudgment and cowardice in leaving Rome rather than fighting. Word reaches him that his enemies have moved to make his exile permanent and his property forfeit; for the first time in his life, the voice that moved the Senate finds nothing to say.
stops.quote: Vos enim video esse miserrimas, quas ego beatissimas semper esse volui — I see you now the most wretched of women, whom I always wished to be the most blessed.
stops.quote_source: Cicero, Epistulae ad Familiares XIV.2, to Terentia
suggested_refs: Thessalonica on the Via Egnatia, where Cicero spent the darkest months of his exile in 58 BC

stops.name: Rome, the Palatine — the house razed, the shrine of Liberty
stops.campa: In Cicero's absence Clodius has his fine house on the Palatine, a monument of his consular dignity, pulled down stone by stone, its portico burned, and its ground consecrated as a templum with a shrine to Libertas raised upon the ruin, so that no vote of the Senate can restore private property to sacred ground. His villas at Tusculum and Formiae are plundered and half wrecked in the same season. It is meant as erasure: the man unmade so completely that even the dirt he stood on is given to a goddess against his return.
suggested_refs: The site of Cicero's Palatine house, razed by Clodius and consecrated with a shrine to Libertas, 58 BC

stops.name: Brundisium — the landing, recalled from exile
stops.campa: The Senate and the tribes, led by Pompey now reconciled to the cause, vote almost unanimously to recall Cicero, and on the fifth of August he lands again at Brundisium to find the whole town turned out to meet him, his daughter Tullia among them. Every city he passes through on the road north sends deputations and holds public thanksgivings as though a magistrate returning in triumph, not a private citizen restored from disgrace, were passing its gates. He will say afterward that Italy itself seemed to lift him up.
stops.quote: Italy took me up on her own shoulders and carried me back into the city.
stops.quote_source: Reported by Plutarch, Life of Cicero 33
suggested_refs: Brundisium (modern Brindisi), where Cicero landed on his recall from exile, 5 August 57 BC

stops.name: Rome — the triumphal entry
stops.campa: Cicero enters Rome by the Capena Gate on the fourth of September, the temple steps of the whole city, he says, crowded with citizens applauding as he passes toward the Capitol to give thanks. The Senate votes that his house on the Palatine and his ruined villas be rebuilt at public expense, and workmen begin clearing the shrine of Libertas from the ground where his atrium stood. He is restored to every honor he held, but the sixteen months away have taught him how thin the republic's gratitude can wear, and how quickly a mob paid in bread can be turned against the man it once carried on its shoulders.
suggested_refs: Cicero's triumphal return to Rome through the Porta Capena, 4 September 57 BC

segments.name: The Memory of Crannon and the Dialogue Years

stops.name: Crannon, Thessaly — Simonides and the founding of memory
stops.campa: In his dialogue On the Orator, written this year in the quiet forced on him by the times, Cicero sets down a story old already in his own youth. At a banquet at Crannon in Thessaly, the poet Simonides sings his host Scopas's praises but wastes half the ode on Castor and Pollux; Scopas pays only half the fee, telling him to collect the rest from the twin gods. A servant calls Simonides outside to two young men; he finds no one, and while he is gone the roof falls, crushing every guest past recognition. Simonides alone, remembering where each man had reclined, names the dead for burial, and so discovers that ordered place is memory's surest hold.
stops.quote: Itaque eis, qui hanc partem ingeni exercerent, locos esse capiendos et ea, quae memoria tenere vellent effingenda animo atque in eis locis conlocanda; sic fore, ut ordinem rerum locorum ordo conservaret, res autem ipsas rerum effigies notaret, atque ut locis pro cera, simulacris pro litteris uteremur — Persons desiring to train this faculty must select localities and form mental images of the things they wish to remember and store those images in the localities, with the result that the arrangement of the localities will preserve the order of the facts, and the images of the facts will designate the facts themselves, and we shall employ the localities and images respectively as a wax writing-tablet and the letters written on it.
stops.quote_source: Cicero, De Oratore II.86.354 (Loeb translation, Sutton and Rackham)
suggested_refs: The banqueting hall of Scopas at Crannon, the founding site of the classical art of memory by places and images
The mnemonic tradition running from Simonides through Cicero to Ramon Llull, Giulio Camillo, Giordano Bruno, and Matteo Ricci
sources: Frances Yates, The Art of Memory

stops.name: Rome — Cicero elected augur, the lituus taken up
stops.campa: Publius Crassus, son of the triumvir, falls with his father's army at Carrhae, and the college of augurs, sixteen priests who read the will of the gods in the flight and cry of birds, elects Cicero to the empty seat, an honor he says he had wanted above every other Roman distinction. He is given the curved staff, the lituus, with which the augur marks out the templum in the sky before he watches it, and he will carry that word's own root, aug-, increase, into a private meditation on why the office is called what it is.
stops.quote: The name augury is thought by the common people to come from the chattering of birds, but more rightly from augendo — that is, from the increase of the commonwealth.
stops.quote_source: Cicero, De Divinatione II.36, in the rendering carried by the Colegio Invisible essay 'Augury'
suggested_refs: The lituus, curved augural staff, and the templum marked in the sky over Rome
The Latin semantic field of aug- (augur, auctoritas, author, inauguration) discussed in the Colegio Invisible essay 'Augury'

stops.name: Tusculum — De Re Publica finished, the Dream of Scipio
stops.campa: Before he must leave for his province, Cicero completes De Re Publica at Tusculum and closes it with the vision he gives to the younger Scipio Aemilianus: the elder Africanus comes to him in a dream and carries him up among the circling spheres, where the music made by their motion, too vast for mortal ears to catch waking, sounds without ceasing. Looking down, Scipio sees the whole earth shrunk to a point, the Roman empire itself no more than a pale mark upon it, and understands that the soul which serves the commonwealth well has a seat prepared for it beyond that turning light.
stops.quote: Iam ipsa terra ita mihi parva visa est, ut me imperii nostri, quo quasi punctum eius attingimus, paeniteret — And the earth itself seemed to me so small that I was ashamed of our empire, which, as it were, touches only a point of its surface.
stops.quote_source: Cicero, De Re Publica VI.16 (Somnium Scipionis)
suggested_refs: The Somnium Scipionis closing De Re Publica, ancestor of Dante's ascent through the Paradiso

segments.name: Cilicia and the Return to War

stops.name: Tarsus, Cilicia — the reluctant proconsul arrives
stops.campa: Under Pompey's new law requiring a gap of years between office and province, Cicero, past fifty and wanting nothing less than to leave Rome and his books, is sent out as proconsul to govern Cilicia, a rough frontier province menaced by Parthia across the Amanus range. He sets up his tribunal at Tarsus and governs, by his own strict account, without taking a single gift, hearing cases himself rather than farming them to freedmen, and writing home constantly to Atticus that he counts the days until his year is done.
suggested_refs: Tarsus, Cicero's provincial capital as governor of Cilicia, 51-50 BC
sources: Cicero, Epistulae ad Familiares III, XV

stops.name: Mount Amanus — hailed imperator
stops.campa: Cicero leads his legions against bandit strongholds in the Amanus range that divides Cilicia from Syria, storming several fortified villages by night assault and routing the free Cilician tribesmen who had never paid tribute to Rome. His soldiers salute him imperator on the field, an honor that in Rome carries the right to petition for a triumph, and for a season the philosopher-consul, more at ease with a stylus than a sword, finds himself, not without some pride he confesses to Atticus, a general in earnest.
suggested_refs: The Amanus mountains (Nur Dağları), scene of Cicero's brief military campaign as governor

stops.name: Pindenissum — the forty-seven day siege
stops.campa: Cicero brings his army against Pindenissum, the strongest fortress of the free Cilicians, said to trust so wholly in its cliffs that no army had ever taken it. He rings it with palisade and ditch, raises earthworks, mantlets, and a great siege tower, and batters it for forty-seven days through the start of winter until the defenders surrender on the Saturnalia. He sells the captives at auction to pay his troops, and writes to Atticus with the plain satisfaction of a man who has done, competently and completely, a piece of work he never wanted.
stops.quote: Cinximus vallo et fossa; aggere maximo, vineis, turre altissima, magna tormentorum copia, multis sagittariis, magno labore, apparatu, multis sauciis nostris, incolumi exercitu negotium confecimus — We ringed it with rampart and ditch; with a great earthwork, mantlets, a very tall tower, a large supply of engines and many archers, with much labour and equipment, with many of our men wounded but the army intact, we finished the business.
suggested_refs: The siege of Pindenissum in the Amanus foothills, December 51 BC, Cicero's one real campaign

stops.name: Dyrrachium — crossing from Caieta to Pompey's camp
stops.campa: Caesar crosses the Rubicon and civil war breaks the uneasy peace Cicero has spent a decade trying to hold together. He hesitates for months, sick with divided loyalty to two men he has praised and feared in turn, before at last taking ship from Caieta on the seventh of June and crossing to Dyrrachium, to Pompey and the Senate's exiled government in the field. He brings no real gift for war and knows it; Pompey's officers mock his caustic jokes at their expense even as they rely on his name to give their cause the color of legitimacy it badly needs.
suggested_refs: Cicero's crossing from Caieta to the Pompeian headquarters at Dyrrachium, June 49 BC

stops.name: Dyrrachium — Pharsalus, the battle he does not fight
stops.campa: Too unwell and too disillusioned to take the field, Cicero stays behind at Dyrrachium while Caesar destroys Pompey's army on the plain of Pharsalus in a single August afternoon. Pompey flees toward Egypt and his death; at the remnant camp Cato and the surviving nobles offer Cicero, as the ranking consular present, command of what is left of the republican cause. He refuses outright, certain now that further war only multiplies the ruin, and turns for home instead, earning Cato's open contempt and his own lasting reputation among the die-hard optimates as the man who quit at the harder half of the fight.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Pharsalus in Thessaly, 9 August 48 BC
Cicero's refusal of the republican command at Dyrrachium, where the news reached him
sources: Plutarch, Life of Cato the Younger

stops.name: Brundisium — Caesar's pardon
stops.campa: Cicero waits out a wretched year at Brundisium, uncertain whether the victorious dictator will treat him as a spared enemy or a dead man walking, until Caesar himself lands there returning from the East. Caesar, seeing the old consular waiting on the road, dismounts, embraces him, and walks with him alone a long way, talking of nothing but ordinary things, before either man mentions the war. It is pardon given as courtesy rather than as favor asked, and Cicero returns to Rome under it, stripped of command but alive, to a public life now conducted entirely at another man's pleasure.
suggested_refs: Caesar's clemency toward Cicero at Brundisium, autumn 47 BC

segments.name: Tusculum, Grief, and the Dictator's Shadow

stops.name: Tusculum — the death of Tullia
stops.campa: A month after bearing a son, Tullia, Cicero's daughter and by far the dearest person in his life, dies at Tusculum. Cicero collapses under a grief his friends have never seen in him and cannot recognize; he abandons Rome, abandons Terentia, whom he divorces within the year, and withdraws first to Atticus's house and then to his own villa at Astura on the shore, alone, walking the wooded island in the little river there for hours, unable to bear the sight of any other face. He begins reading every Greek consolation ever written on the death of a child, and finds none of them sufficient.
stops.quote: In hac solitudine careo omnium conloquio, cumque mane me in silvam abstrusi densam et asperam, non exeo inde ante vesperum — In this solitude I speak with no one, and when in the morning I have hidden myself away in a thick and rugged wood, I do not come out of it before evening.
stops.quote_source: Cicero, Letters to Atticus XII.15, written from Astura
suggested_refs: Astura, the wooded river-island retreat where Cicero secluded himself after Tullia's death, and the lost Consolatio he wrote there

stops.name: Tusculum — the dialogues of grief and old age
stops.campa: Out of the worst year of his life Cicero drives himself back to work at Tusculum, writing at a pace that astonishes even Atticus: the Tusculan Disputations on facing death and pain, On the Nature of the Gods, On Old Age for his friend Atticus, On Friendship in memory of the Scipio he never knew, all composed within months of one another. He turns Greek philosophy's whole vocabulary into workable Latin as he goes, inventing words the language did not have, so that Rome, exiled from politics under a dictator, might at least possess a philosophy of its own to suffer with.
suggested_refs: The Tusculan Disputations, De Natura Deorum, De Senectute, and De Amicitia, all written at Tusculum in the year of grief, 45 BC

stops.name: Rome, the Curia of Pompey — the Ides of March
stops.campa: Cicero sits among the senators in the hall built onto Pompey's theatre, called that day to a meeting of the Senate, and watches Caesar, dictator for life, go down under twenty-three blows from men he had pardoned. He had no part in the plot and learns of it only as it happens, but Brutus, lifting his bloody dagger clear of the body, is said to call out Cicero's name before any other, hailing the recovery of the republic's liberty in the one voice in Rome that liberty most needs. Cicero will spend what is left of his own life trying to make that shout true.
suggested_refs: The Curia of Pompey at the Largo di Torre Argentina, site of Caesar's assassination
Brutus raising his dagger and calling Cicero's name, as recorded by Plutarch and Appian

stops.name: Rome, the Temple of Concord — the First Philippic
stops.campa: Six months after the Ides, with Antony ruling Rome by decree and Caesar's assassins scattered or besieged, Cicero returns to the Senate meeting in the Temple of Concord and delivers the first of what he will come to call, in homage to Demosthenes against Philip of Macedon, his own Philippics. It is measured still, more warning than attack, but it announces to Antony and to Rome both that the old consular voice, silent through most of the dictatorship, has decided to speak again in its own name, whatever the cost of speaking proves to be.
suggested_refs: The Temple of Concord in the Roman Forum, where the First Philippic was delivered, 2 September 44 BC

stops.name: Rome — De Officiis, a father's last book
stops.campa: Even as the Philippics escalate, Cicero finds time to write De Officiis, three books on moral duty addressed to his son Marcus, studying at Athens and, Cicero worries, drinking more than he studies. It becomes his last completed work and his clearest statement of what a life owed to the republic should look like: that nothing base can ever truly be expedient, that no gain is worth the wrong of taking from one man to give to another. He sends it east not knowing it will outlive every regime he has fought to save, copied and argued over for two thousand years after Rome itself has fallen.
suggested_refs: De Officiis, Cicero's final philosophical work, addressed to his son at Athens, autumn 44 BC

stops.name: Rome — the war of the Philippics
stops.campa: Through the winter Cicero delivers Philippic after Philippic, fourteen in all, driving the Senate to declare Antony a public enemy and to back the young Octavian, Caesar's heir, as a counterweight against him, a wager Cicero believes he can manage and later, too late, discovers he cannot. He speaks now almost daily, at nearly sixty, with the same reckless candor as in his consulship and four decades of political memory behind it, staking everything on the belief that the republic, badly wounded, is still worth this last unequal fight against a soldier with legions and no such scruples.
stops.quote: Quis tum nobis, quis populo Romano optulit hunc divinum adulescentem deus? — What god was it who then gave us, who gave the Roman people, this divine young man?
suggested_refs: The fourteen Philippics against Mark Antony, delivered September 44 to April 43 BC

stops.name: Rome — the Second Triumvirate, the proscription
stops.campa: Octavian, Antony, and Lepidus meet near Bononia, patch up their rivalry, and form a triumvirate with absolute power, sealed at once by a proscription list of enemies to be killed without trial and their property seized. Antony, unforgiving of the Philippics, insists on Cicero's name; Octavian, who owes Cicero his very political start, is said to argue two days before yielding him up in exchange for an uncle of Antony's own the young man wants dead. Cicero's name goes onto the list with his brother Quintus and his nephew, and the household begins, too late, to run.
suggested_refs: The proscription lists of the Second Triumvirate, November 43 BC, on which Cicero's name was placed

stops.name: Formiae — the flight ends, the death
stops.campa: Cicero is carried in a litter toward the coast at Caieta, meaning to take ship at last for Macedonia and Brutus, but turns back to his villa at Formiae, worn out and telling his slaves to let happen what the gods will. The centurion Herennius and the tribune Popillius, once defended by Cicero himself in a parricide case, find him there and force the litter-bearers to set it down. Cicero pushes his head out toward the swords himself, sparing his men further struggle, and speaks the last words the tradition preserves of the greatest voice Rome ever produced.
stops.quote: There is nothing proper about what you are doing, soldier, but do try to kill me properly.
stops.quote_source: Reported by Plutarch, Life of Cicero 48
suggested_refs: Cicero's villa at Formiae, where he was overtaken and killed, 7 December 43 BC
The tower tomb on the Via Appia at Formia traditionally called the Tomb of Cicero, which marks the spot
sources: Livy, fragment ap. Seneca the Elder, Suasoriae VI.17

stops.name: Rome, the Rostra — the head and hands, Fulvia's needle
stops.campa: Herennius carries the severed head and, on Antony's order, the right hand that wrote the Philippics back to Rome. Antony has them nailed up on the Rostra itself, the platform from which Cicero had spoken against Catiline, against the triumvirs' predecessors, against Antony's own edicts, so that his silence now stands exactly where his voice once had. Fulvia, Antony's wife and Clodius's widow before him, is said to take the head into her lap, spit on it, pull out the tongue, and pierce it through and through with the pins from her own hair, before it is set up for Rome to see.
suggested_refs: The Rostra in the Roman Forum, where Cicero's head and right hand were displayed, December 43 BC
